paragraphs: Biodiversity and structure analyses of microbial communities

DNA of the bacterial and archaeal genomes was separated from the digestate according to the instruction manual of the OMEGA kit and subjected to agarose gel electrophoresis to perform integrity determination. The microorganisms in the digestate were analyzed based on 16S rRNA gene sequencing. The structure of the bacterial communities was evaluated with two rounds of PCR amplification. First, the primers 341F (5'-CCT ACG GGN GGC WGC AG-3') and 805R (5'-GAC TAC HVG GGT ATC TAA TCC -3') were used and 15 μL of 2 × Taq master Mix, 1 μL of Bar-PCR primer (μM), 10-20 ng of genomic DNA, and 30 μL of H2O were used as the amplification systems. Second, Illumina Bridge PCR-compatible primers were applied and 15 μL of 2 × Taq master Mix, 1 μL of Primer F (10 μM), 1 μL of Primer R (10 μM), 20 ng of PCR products, and 30 μL of H2O were used to form the amplification system. The structure of the archaeal community was studied with three rounds of PCR amplification. In the first round, M-340F (5'-CCC TAY GGG GYG CAS CAG-3') and GY1ST-1000R (5'-GGC CAT GCA CYW CYT CTC-3') were used as primers and 15 μL 2 × Taq master Mix, 1 μL Bar-PCR Primer F (10 μM), 1 μL Primer R (10 μM), 10-20 ng Genomic DNA, and 30 μL H2O were used to form the amplification system. In the second round, the products obtained from the first round were used for the amplification, and although the constituents were the same, the primers were 349F (5'-GYG CAS CAG KCG MGA AW-3') and 806R (5'-GGA CTA CVS GGG TAT CTA AT-3'). In the third round, Illumina bridge PCR-compatible primers were used and 15 μL 2 × Taq master Mix, 1 μL Primer F (10 μM), 1 μL Primer R (10 μM), 20 ng PCR products, and 30 μL H2O were loaded as the amplification system. The PCR products were detected by agarose electrophoresis. The DNA was purified and recovered and then mixed in equal amounts for sequencing. The resulting sequences were used to remove chimeras and nonspecifically amplified sequences to collect the quality sequences for clustering as operational taxonomic units (OTUs), according to the lowest similarity level of 97%.

Three groups including CM, LI, and SI groups, each represented in relative abundance of phylum level, were recognized (Fig. S2). Obvious microbial succession in RA of these phyla could be observed before and after AD. As the most dominant phylum in LI agent, Firmicutes gradually reduced from 97.3% of RA in LI to 61.8% of RA in anaerobic LI pretreated sample, and 38.1% in aerobic pretreated sample. The results showed that the possible substitute for anaerobic condition with aerobic condition during LI carried disadvantages for enrichment of Firmicutes. The key step to convert lignocellulose into methane was widely known as hydrolysis, while Firmicutes had been extensively investigated as a phylum possessing a number of cellulolytic bacteria (Lin et al., 2017), which had the same important status as protein ammoniating bacteria and other fermenting bacteria. Therefore, LI pretreatment under aerobic condition was unable to degrade the cellulose of giant grass more efficiently, thus higher EMY was not resulted. In the corresponding digestate, the RA of Firmicutes accounted to 31.7% and 34.5% for anaerobic and aerobic condition, respectively, which was less than that of untreated. The loss of RA in Firmicutes from pretreated sample to digestate could be due to the thermophilic characteristic Firmicutes had (Lin et al., 2017). Different from Firmicutes, Proteobacteria was only 2.6% of RA, and increased to 37.1% of RA in LI1 and 60.4% of RA in LI2, but largely decreased to 6.9% of RA in LI4 and 9.9% of RA in LI5. The diminishment in the RA of Proteobacteria might be caused the extinction of some Proteobacteria members during AD process. Meanwhile, Bacteroidetes had the largest RA of 42.9% and 36.2% in LI4 and LI5, respectively, instead of the second largest RA of 33.3% in untreated. Bacteroidetes had been identified as the relatively abundant phylum during mesophilic AD process, by which the preliminary decomposition of organic substances could be achieved and some bacteria belonging to Bacteroidetes utilized protein (Han et al., 2016). Collectively, Firmicutes was detected to be showing insignificant difference at anaerobic or aerobic condition for LI, while the digestate of anaerobic LI pretreatment enriched more Bacteroidetes. The result given probably played a critical role in the highest methane production from anaerobic LI pretreatment during LI groups.

Firmicutes (about 37.0%-40.1%) always taken the predominance within the total bacteria in SI3, SI4, SI5, followed by Bacteroidete (25.3%-30.6%), with the resting determined as Proteobacteria (9.9%-13.6%), Chloroflexi (9.9%-12.0%), Synergistetes (5.21%-5.61%), and some hardly undetectable phyla. The RA of Firmicutes did have no obvious difference, but the RA of Bacteroidetes, Chloroflexi, and Synergistetes in SI4 were higher than SI3 and SI5. Chloroflexi correlated well with the digestion of carbohydrates and amino acids (Yi et al., 2014), while Synergistetes was responsible for acetate conversion. A leader in this case might resulted in the higher EMY for anaerobic condition for SI pretreatment. The digestate from CM group position showed similar distribution in the RA of these bacteria phyla as that from SI groups, except for Chloroflexi, which was lower than CM5 for CM4. This finding perhaps was strongly related to the highest EMY within CM groups occurred at an oxygen loading of 10 mL/g VS. Apart from that, it had been reported that a better hydrolysis performance usually accompanied by a higher ratio of Firmicutes to Bacteroidetes, which could be as an explanation for higher VFAs concentrations produced from CM and SI groups than LI groups (Guellert et al., 2016). Furthermore, a higher RA of Chloroflexi were generally observed for AD digestates from CM and SI groups in contrast with LI group. This might be responsible for the higher EMYs produced from CM and SI groups because acetate and some short fatty acids was normally generated from the conversion of several sugars through Chloroflexi (Gulhane et al., 2017).

The RA of archaea in the digesters from LI, SI, and CM groups exhibited generally similar distribution in phylum level (Fig. S3). It could be seen that Euryarchaeota and Crenarchaeota dominated always throughout AD process, especially Euryarchaeota whose RA was even more than 50% or more. This was indicating these two phyla assumed primary responsibility for methane production. Besides, the change in pretreatment agent and oxygen loading apparently was less of a factor to influence the archaeal species, but causing the difference in the RA of each archaea at phylum level. For instance, the RA of Euryarchaeota during LI4 (74.76%) experienced an increase up to 89.64% in LI5, accompanied with a drop in the RA of Crenarchaeota from 21.44% to 9.63%. Likewise, SI4 and SI5 displayed similar situation but to a different extent. Euryarchaeota was widely considered to participate in the greenhouse gas generation, additionally with the capacity of methane oxidization (Michaelis et al., 2002). Therefore, the superior performance of these two phyla in terms of LI and SI pretreatment process at microaerobic condition likely resulted in the decrease in methane production as observed in Fig 3, in contrast with that from corresponding group at anaerobic condition. Contrarily, the RA of Euryarchaeotain during CM4 (65.91%) had shifted to 62.5% in CM5. This might be closed to the observation that microaerobic CM pretreatment for giant grass was found to have higher EMY than anaerobic CM pretreatment.
